This started off as a reply to a post in here, but it got... long. Gonna post it to the main thread instead, since it might get some more visibility:

*stands on soapbox*

I'm an OC machine. I make music. Lots of it. Been doing it for over a decade. Anonymously, too, mind-you (although not always). I've gone to some lengths to make sure my real identity isn't tied to what I do. No reason in particular, either; just want the work to speak for itself.

Have you seen the rules in /v/music or /v/listentothis? Wait... I just went there to copy+paste the fucking loooooooong diatribe that was on the right panel, and it appears to have vanished. Either they're smartening up, or something happened that I'm not aware of. They had restrictions like, "If you post your own music, don't do it more than once a month or it'll be considered spam and you'll be banned", etc.

Maybe I'll give it a shot. But just wanted to add an echo to the chamber, and reinforce that: no, you're not alone in thinking like this. For whatever reason, musicians and cartoonists are especially ostracized for sharing their creations. It's like no one wants to hear from you until you're already famous and someone that "matters". Otherwise, you're just a snake trying to take advantage of people... by sharing our creations with them... because we thought they'd like it... somehow.

Bitch, how do you think anyone's going to get popular "organically" unless you take a chance and listen to something that isn't backed up by a huge record label, or being big-upped by someone who's already an icon? Not everyone can be friends with Dr. Dre or know someone who works at Warp Records. I don't necessarily want to make music my career (obviously it'd be nice, but not the ultimate goal), and don't wanna spend my life kissing ass and working up the corporate Music Business™ ladder. However...

There was a time when I wanted to be a professional musician. I even have my own Beatport store page and everything. You can listen to/buy some of my "commercial" tracks on Google Play, iTunes/Apple Music, TraxSource, Spotify, etc. Have releases on a few underground labels... let me tell you, that shit is daunting. I gave up making the type of music I love, and ended up pushing out EDM-style abominations in order to garner attention, just because I wanted people to appreciate my musical talents. And you wanna know the sad part?

It was working. That made the whole thing even sadder, and soon stopped releasing anything altogether. These days, I dump a few tracks at a time, here and there, on different profiles— under different names. Some stuff has a few thousand plays, others maybe five.

The internet promised to give us all an equal footing, but it's done exactly the opposite. Brand Name™ artists' representatives carpet bomb social media with millions of dollars worth of targeted advertising and exposure. Those of us without these resources are left to our own devices, in a largely inhospitable landscape, at that.

This whole, "shut up, no one wants to listen to you music. It's obviously shitty, because if it wasn't, you'd already be famous" mentality is really prevalent; unless you pander to the lowest common denominator or aren't trying to do anything truly unique (a.k.a following the herd), then you're good.

But I can't do that. I'm the type of person that rolls their eyes at predictable plot twists in shitty movies, except that it happens with music as well. I try to do things that are different, and there's really no place for "different" in today's musical world. Hell, the last recourse I have where this content might possibly, sometimes; in the exact, specific, opportune context where it would be accepted are sites like reddit/voat. And srsly guise, fuck reddit.

I know this really only relates to one specific person, about one specific topic; but I have an inkling that this situation translates over to a lot of different, creative, fields. Unless you already have the status quo's support, you're nothing. And everyone treats you as nothing.

*and thus ends the rant*

I guess all I'm saying is: there's probably lots of people here on voat with lots of OC to share, we just know that sometimes it isn't worth the hassle.

Hence the reason my contributions are limited to what I find on the web or comments. That's it. My writing is available if anyone would like to read it same as my photography. It just will never be posted here or any other aggregate site.

Did science yet come up with a way to definitively test your DNA for mental diseases?

I know for a fact that my entire family is fucked up (and thus, so am I), but without them going to a shrink's office (won't ever happen), I can't be too sure of exactly what they transmitted to me.

Have you considered just going to a psych yourself? It'd be far more accurate than trying to get a bunch of other people to go (and it can take months or years to get a firm diagnosis), and then getting them to honestly tell you what if anything they were diagnosed with.

I don't have money or transportation. Plus, I'm wary of the whole subjective-interview thing (and the demonstrated link between psych dr's getting kickbacks from pharma). I'm more interested in physical, concrete evidence, like do I have something abnormal in an MRI/PET/EEG scan associated with this or that, or an abnormality in my genetic code associated with this or that. But again, I not only can't afford it, I don't have a car or anyone to take me there.

I don't know why mental disorders have been so far behind other diagnoses in terms of concrete physical evidence like other diseases are. I mean, you go and get a blood test and they determine you have diabetes or anemia or AIDS, and they can now determine that someone has Alzheimer's or Parkinson's using brain scans. You can find the BRCA gene with genetic sequencing. Why aren't brain scans and genetic testing requested for schizophrenia, or manic-depression, or PTSD? Is it just the cost and insurance's unwillingness to pay, or is it really not that certain yet what "crazy" looks like in a genome sequence or brain scan? Or is it the Godwin taboo about eugenics and shock therapy, and this new idea of a mental state being a "fluid identity" rather than a physical disorder?

I think diagnosis of mental disorders is so far behind for the simple reason that our brains are incredibly complicated, our tools for inspecting them are comparatively primitive, and even if we had all of the info we really don't understand how human minds work yet.

Think of it as being like trying to figure out why your computer is rendering a particular web site in the wrong font, by taking off the side of your computer case and using a thermometer to measure the temperature of different chips on the motherboard. You can detect things like Alzheimer's because there are macroscopic physical changes associated with them (like looking in your computer case and hmm, someone's yoinked one of the hard drives - that's why those files are gone!) and things like bipolar disorder because there are significant chemical changes (like, I dunno, your power supply is bouncing between 3V and 6V on the 5V rail, to stick with the computer analogy). But it's many orders of magnitude harder to figure out that a font file got corrupted and so your OS is defaulting to one of the stock fonts, especially if you don't know what a font is, or an OS, or a web browser, or what format the hard drive is in, etc. etc.

As for what 'crazy' looks like in a gene sequence or an fMRI, we don't even have a proper definition of what 'crazy' IS in the general case. It's just the human equivalent of 'the computer did something funny and I don't understand why'.
